message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**Summary:** The price increases are reasonable, and the competitor positioning holds up. But the paper has three substantive problems:

- **It ignores the 12% beef price rise it reports in section 4.** That rise eats about a third of the projected gain.
- **The risotto claim is backwards.** Risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu (80%), not the weakest, and replacing it could *reduce* profit.
- **It uses a seasonal baseline that will distort the monitoring.**

There's also a possible VAT issue that could shrink the figures further, and a factual slip about the number of trading days.

## 1. The beef cost rise isn't in the projection

Section 4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Applying 12% to the full plate cost gives an upper-bound estimate:

| Dish | Current food cost | +12% | Extra per plate | Plates/week | Extra cost/week |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 | £4.70 | £0.50 | 260 | £131 |
| Steak | £10.40 | £11.65 | £1.25 | 120 | £150 |
| **Total** | | | | | **≈ £281** |

The true figure is a little lower, since buns, chips and sides aren't beef. Even so:

- The weekly gain falls from £810 to **about £530**, or about **£27,500 a year rather than £42,100**.
- The main-course margin stays at **about 70%**, not 71%. Excluding specials, it's about 69.9% now, 71.3% after the price rises, and about 69.7% once beef costs are included. So the price rises mostly **offset the beef increase**. They don't improve the margin.

That's still a good reason to raise prices, but the paper should present it as protecting the margin, not restoring it.

## 2. The risotto has the best margin, not the weakest

| Dish | Margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80%** (highest) | **£11.20** |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 |

The table is right; the text in section 5.2 and the author's description misread it. The risotto also ties with specials for lowest sales (90 each), rather than being lowest on its own.

The replacement could also cost money. Specials currently run at a **64%** margin. If the new vegetarian special performs like a typical special at £14, its gross profit per plate falls from £11.20 to about £8.96. On 90 plates a week, that's **about £200 a week, or £10,500 a year, less**.

There may still be good reasons to change the dish, such as staleness, seasonality or kitchen workload. But the paper should argue those reasons, and set a food-cost target for the special of about £2.80 or less to protect the margin. If the risotto is the only vegetarian main, keep a strong vegetarian option.

## 3. Check VAT

UK menu prices normally include **20% VAT**. Table 1's margins appear to be calculated on the VAT-inclusive price: for fish and chips, (£16.50 − £5.10) ÷ £16.50 = 69%. If so:

- Each £1 menu increase adds only **about £0.83** in actual revenue.
- £810 a week becomes **about £675**. After the beef costs, that's **about £395 a week, or roughly £20,500 a year**.
- All the margins in Table 1 are overstated. Fish and chips is about 63% on a net-of-VAT basis.

If your accounts already use VAT-inclusive margins consistently, say so explicitly. Either way, the owners should know which basis is being used.

## 4. The monitoring baseline is seasonal

January and February are typically a restaurant's quietest months. Comparing April and May volumes against them will probably show **growth**, which could hide a real drop caused by the price rises. Better options:
- compare against **April and May 2025**, adjusting for any known changes, or
- track each dish's **share of total mains** rather than absolute plates sold, which is less affected by season.

Also set a **threshold for action**, such as "if steak volume falls more than X%, review the price."

## 5. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** The restaurant is open **Wednesday to Sunday, five days**, but the recommendation says "six trading days a week."
- **Loyal customers.** A 60% repeat rate does suggest loyalty, but regular guests are also the most likely to notice the rises. "Absorb a pound or two" is a judgement call, and the paper should present it as one.
- **Weekday lunch.** The paper calls lunch "a small share" of main-course sales. Give the actual figure, since Friday and Saturday dinners are under half.
- **Fish prices** are volatile. The paper could note the risk to the most popular dish.

## What holds up

- Table 1's margins and the total of 1,050 plates a week are correct.
- All three new prices sit below the competitor midpoints: £17.50 against £17.98, £16.00 against £16.50, and £28.00 against £29.50.
- The paper is correct that current prices are the lowest in the competitor group.
- The weekly uplift before costs is correct: 310 + 260 + 240 = £810, which is £42,120 a year.
- Weekly monitoring by dish is a sensible approach.

## Recommended changes before the owners decide

1. Include the beef cost rise in the projection, and present the price rises as protecting the margin.
2. Correct the risotto analysis, and set a margin target for any replacement special.
3. State whether the figures include VAT, and recalculate on a net-of-VAT basis if they do.
4. Use a seasonally comparable baseline and set action thresholds.
5. Fix the number of trading days.
6. Consider raising the burger and steak further. Both are still well below the competitor midpoints, and they're the dishes hit by the beef increase.

The price rises are justified and probably still worthwhile. But the realistic benefit is perhaps **£20,000–£28,000 a year**, depending on the VAT basis, and removing the risotto works against the paper's own goal.
